k689: Vlorë has doubled in three years in parts. A large share of that is an airport premium — the expectation that Vlorë International will open and bring direct European traffic. The airport is a real project. It is also not open, and its timeline has moved.
k690: If it opens on schedule, today's prices are defensible. If it slips again, you have paid for it twice.
k692: The capital's top-end towers at roughly 5,000-10,000 euros per square metre have two problems. The first is arithmetic: gross yields under 3% do not compensate for the risk of owning an illiquid asset in a small market. The second is observable — commentary on the Tirana skyline has repeatedly noted how many of these units sit empty.
k693: Empty units are not automatically a crisis; second homes and stores of value are legitimate. But they are a warning about exit. You need a buyer with the same motivation to get out at your price, and that buyer pool is small.
k695: The marina district is the most aggressively marketed development on the central coast. Our reservations are about structure rather than location: reports of settlement in some blocks, a sales model that leans heavily on pre-sales funding later phases, and a port relocation that underpins much of the pitch and has not happened.
k696: Pre-sale-funded development is normal. It is also the model that leaves buyers exposed when volumes fall — and volumes are falling.
k697: Paskuqan and Kamëz new build at around 1,200 euros
k698: These northern Tirana areas have seen new build asking prices converge on what Astir commands. The two are not comparable. Title risk is materially higher, and the social and transport infrastructure is thinner. Paying an Astir price for a Paskuqan title is the clearest example on this list of a price that has simply detached.
k700: Shëngjin's northern frontier carries a "last undeveloped beach" premium. It also carries live legal proceedings concerning construction on the dunes, and documented coastal erosion. Where a legal process is unresolved, the honest position is that the risk is unpriced rather than that the property is bad — but unpriced risk at a premium price is a poor combination.
k701: What to do with this list
k703: Ask what event the price assumes, and get the current status of that event in writing.
k704: Compare the price per square metre to the rent the unit actually earns today, not to what a neighbouring zone charges.
k705: Check the title and the permit before anything else, especially near dunes, protected areas and reclassified agricultural land.
k706: If a zone here still looks right for you after that, buy it — with a discount that reflects what you have just found. Our objection is almost never to the place. It is to the price the place is being sold at in 2026.

Farkë-Lundër and the Rruga e Elbasanit corridor for gated villas, and Don Bosko and Fresku for gentrifying value.
k751: If you want walkable, loud, and central: Blloku and Pazari i Ri
k752: <s0>Blloku</s0> is the former Communist-era closed quarter, now the city's densest concentration of bars, boutiques and offices — the district table rates it 8.5/10 on prestige, walkability and safety, and marks its real trade-off just as clearly: traffic, noise, parking, and a rental yield that's capped because the price has already outrun the rent. About 27% of buyers in the immediate centre are non-residents, drawn by the same liquidity that makes it easy to resell.
k753: <s0>Pazari i Ri</s0>, the renovated 2016 market square, is the city's best Airbnb zone by a clear margin — tourist foot traffic, restaurants, a genuine "old town" feel — but that's also its downside for a resident: it's a district built around visitors passing through, not neighbours settling in.
k754: If you're raising a family: Komuna e Parisit and Myslym Shyri
k755: Komuna e Parisit sits beside Tirana's Grand Park, ringed by embassies and families rather than nightlife — the KB's own note calls it "family-prime without Blloku's noise," and its main complaint is parking, not safety or schools. Myslym Shyri is the more affordable version of the same idea: a shopping street that doubles as "the most convenient residential centre for families," with the highest local liquidity of any district DomLivo tracks, meaning it's also easy to resell if your family's needs change.
k756: If you want the villa life: Farkë/Lundër and the embassy corridor
k757: Above the apartment market entirely sits a gated-villa segment: <s1>Farkë/Lundër</s1>, near Lake Farka, anchors it: Rolling Hills, Piccadilly, Farka Lake Shore and others aimed at expat management and diplomatic tenants. The Rruga e Elbasanit corridor, where the US, Dutch and Spanish embassies sit, is the other end of the same segment: the most expensive lots in the city, almost nothing new built there in years. Neither is a walk-to-everything district — both trade proximity for space, quiet and a gate.
k758: If you're watching a neighbourhood change in real time: Don Bosko and Fresku
k759: Don Bosko is dense, lively, and genuinely gentrifying — cafés, a market, a school (GDQ), and rents running €100–300 a month cheaper than Blloku for a similar flat. <s1>Fresku</s1>, on the eastern slope toward Dajti, rose 16–27% after a new road connected it to the city's Grand Ring; it also has the cleanest air of anywhere on this list, being furthest from the traffic-heavy centre. Its one real weakness is structural: the whole district leans on that single road link, so anything that disrupts it disrupts the district.
k760: If your budget is tight and you still want an identity: Kombinat and Ali Demi
k761: <s0>Kombinat</s0> is a 1950s textile-workers' town, six kilometres out, with new builds from €1,000/m² — the cheapest district on this list with a real history behind it rather than an anonymous new-build front. <s2>Ali Demi</s2> is "old Tirana" in a different sense: older housing stock, the Continental Hospital and the Bektashi World Centre nearby, gentrifying at a genuinely good price-to-centre ratio.
k762: The districts worth a second look before committing
k763: <s0>Astir/Unaza e Re</s0> carries the largest new-build pipeline in the southwest, aimed mostly at young families priced out of the centre — and with it, the city's clearest oversupply risk; reference prices there jumped 76% in 2023 alone, a pace few districts can sustain. <s2>Kashar</s2>, the western corridor toward Durrës, is betting on the Tirana–Durrës railway to turn a "dormitory suburb by the highway" into something with its own identity; until that finishes, it's exactly what it sounds like. Both are fine as an affordability trade, less fine as a bet that the neighbourhood becomes something more before you need to sell.
k764: None of this replaces walking the street yourself at the hour you'd actually be there — a Friday night in Blloku and a Tuesday morning in Komuna e Parisit tell you more than any rating does. <s1>Once you've picked a district, the purchase mechanics are the same wherever you land</s1>: notary, ASHK, the same checks on the title regardless of the neighbourhood's personality.
